div.head: Chapter 14
div.p: Now it remains to be seen how the Spaniards observed, in their first entry or first foothold that they set in those Indies and in every part of them, the said order of natural and divine law in its parts; and thus the justice with which they entered will become apparent.

As regards the first part, then, which was to enter in peace: their entry and entrance was not as of cruel men without mercy who had received great injuries and wrongs from others and wished to avenge themselves by making deliberate and conspicuous massacres and devastations alone; but as of savage and irrational beasts: as tigers upon children to devour them; as ravenous and rabid wolves upon the most gentle and innocent lambs; entering each town killing and tearing apart men and women, children and old people, lords and subjects alike, with no distinction of age or sex or dignity; many times falling upon them unawares in their homes and in their beds in the dead of night, setting fire to the houses of those who did not come out quickly enough; and those who fled from the fire found the swords waiting for them there that gutted them and cut them to pieces. Many times, when the Indians came out joyfully bearing gifts of food and gold and rich jewels, cotton and other things, to receive them, the Spaniards fell upon them, claiming that they came with evil intent and that the welcome was feigned, in order to justify making those taken alive slaves made in a just war. Other times still, having assured them that they should come down from the mountains where they had fled in fear, and that no harm or hurt would be done to them, those who trusted in their word and came to put themselves in their impious hands were killed or enslaved. And this was the wickedness of our own people, who never kept faith or truth or any word of safe conduct they had given to those peoples. There was a tyrant who bore the surname Guerra — War — and when certain towns came to submit to him and serve him with gifts of peace, he answered that he wanted no peace because his name was War, and therefore he would not receive them in peace but must take them by war; and so he made innumerable slaves. One of the things that we tyrants have been most bent upon, after filling ourselves with gold, was making those innocent peoples slaves, to have them and use them entirely at our will.

They tested their swords upon them, wagering who could split an Indian in half or cut off his head with a single stroke; they threw them to fierce dogs trained for that purpose, who tore them to pieces in a heartbeat. They packed the bohíos — the thatched houses the Indians commonly had — with people: men and women, pregnant and new mothers, children and old people; and set fire to them, where everyone burned. They placed them on certain beds made on low forked stakes, with rods lashed over them in the manner of a grill, and upon these they bound them two by two and three by three and four by four, and beneath they lit a fierce fire, and there they roasted them alive. And this I saw with my own mortal eyes. There was a tyrant who, in order to make them give him gold, seized the king and lord of the land and one of the greatest lords, if there were more than one who ruled it; he had him roasted in the manner described; and the tyrant himself strolled back and forth, praying the rosary, and from time to time would say: "Add more fire and turn him on the other side." They hanged many women, and the nursing infants they hanged from their mothers' feet. Others they impaled on stakes from below upward, and they split open their wombs and thrust the babies in headfirst, where the infants were immediately drowned in their mothers' blood.

Our Christians — if they were that in any sense at all — always harbored a very common purpose, in every place they entered, with which Satan had invested their souls: to carry out some conspicuous and cruel massacre and slaughter, to breed and root their terror deep into the souls of those gentle sheep and lambs, so that their dreadful name might thunder throughout the whole land; and thus, at the mere word "Christians," the flesh of the people trembled, not moderately but beyond all that can be expressed.

It is true before the Just Judge who shall judge us, that if I were to recount all the kinds of torments and their number that our people have done and do today to those nations — who never did us harm, but rather many signal kindnesses — in the wars and in all the rest of daily life, of those who escaped from them with their lives, no great quantity of paper would suffice, nor a considerable portion of one's life to relate it; and I affirm that I do not tell or exaggerate so much as one part in a thousand. Such, then, is the peace that the Spaniards brought to that New World, and thus they observed the divine and natural order. Let the reader judge from this, then, whether it is well proved that the first entry or entrance of the Spaniards into those Indies and into every one of their parts was and has been tyrannical.
